Parched
PARCHT
adj. and v. (past part.)
From parch, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Latin persiccare, to dry thoroughly. Webster 1828: scorched; dried to extremity by heat. Scripture uses it of ground without water, and of grain roasted at the fire — the ordinary food of harvesters and armies.

Biblical Definition

Parched in Scripture means dried by heat, and it names two things: land without water, and corn roasted over a fire. Of the land, Jeremiah gives the fate of the man who trusts in man: he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited (Jeremiah 17:6) — and the contrast four verses later is the tree planted by the waters, which does not see when heat cometh. Isaiah promises the reversal: the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes (Isaiah 35:7). Of the food, parched corn was what a reaper ate in the field, and Boaz hands it to a foreign widow gleaning behind his men: he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left (Ruth 2:14). And the law forbids eating it until the firstfruits have been offered: ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God (Leviticus 23:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PARCHED as scorched; dried to extremity by heat; and of grain, roasted or dried by the fire, as parched corn.

expand to see more

PARCHED, pp. — Scorched; dried to extremity; deprived of moisture by heat.

Of grain, roasted or dried at the fire; as parched corn, a common food in the East.

Applied to land, denoting ground burnt dry and unfit for cultivation.

PARCH, v.t. — To burn the surface of; to scorch; to dry to extremity.

Of uncertain origin; perhaps from Latin persiccare, to dry thoroughly.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 17:6 — "For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited."

Isaiah 35:7 — "And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes."

Ruth 2:14 — "And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left."

Leviticus 23:14 — "And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings."

Modern Corruption

Jeremiah 17 sets trusting in man against trusting in the LORD and describes the first as a curse, which is the plainest biblical refutation of the therapeutic and political habit of locating a person’s hope in human help.

expand to see more

The passage is built as a pair. Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD — and he shall inhabit the parched places, in a salt land not inhabited, and shall not see when good comes. Then: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD… For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters… and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought. Both men face the same weather; one does not notice the good and the other does not notice the heat. Nothing here forbids the ordinary use of doctors, counsellors, friends, or magistrates — Scripture commends all of them. What it forbids is making flesh the arm, and Jeremiah adds the reason in the next breath: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?

Ruth 2:14 is one of the small kindnesses in Scripture that carries a large doctrine. Boaz calls a destitute Moabite widow to the reapers’ meal, seats her among his own workers, and hands her parched corn until she has eaten and left some over. She was outside the covenant by birth, poor, foreign, and gleaning by a legal charity she had no natural claim to. The man who fed her became her kinsman-redeemer, and their great-grandson was David. It is a picture worth setting against every account of grace as something earned or owed: the redeemer feeds the one he will redeem, before she knows what he intends.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qali (H7039), parched corn; charer (H2787), to be scorched; sharab (H8273), parched ground, a mirage; tsimmaon (H6774), thirsty ground.

expand to see more

Hebrew qali (H7039) — parched or roasted grain; the reapers’ food that Boaz gave to Ruth (Ruth 2:14).

Hebrew charer (H2787) — to be scorched, burned; behind the parched places in the wilderness (Jeremiah 17:6).

Hebrew sharab (H8273) — parched ground, and also the shimmering mirage of the desert; the parched ground shall become a pool (Isaiah 35:7).

Hebrew tsimmaon (H6774) — thirsty ground; the companion term in the same verse.

Hebrew melechah (H4420) — a salt land, barrenness; in a salt land and not inhabited (Jeremiah 17:6).

Usage

"He shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness (Jeremiah 17:6) — the man who makes flesh his arm."

"The parched ground shall become a pool (Isaiah 35:7) — the promised reversal, in the habitation of dragons."

"He reached her parched corn (Ruth 2:14) — a redeemer feeding the woman he would redeem."
